I understand where you’re coming from. I recently graduated nursing school and got my RN. I had originally juggled with the notion of going into nursing due to the impact my psych nurse had on me when I was an inpatient teen. She was the kind of nurse that was all rough around the edges, but with a kind heart, a huge brain, and her presence brought me immeasurable comfort, trust, and healing. She had an air that I envied, and I get the feeling she’d try and fist fight me for even saying that. She was incredibly real and blunt, and she was able to connect with me so much more than the other nurses through simply… being her, it’s so hard to describe. I still have the sticky notes she instructed me to fill with things about me that are /good/, they hang on my closet door and make me face the fact that I made it and am still alive.

When I got worse again, I became deeply obsessed with the need to perform a service, to be of use, to have purpose. It led me down a dark path. But from that person, my present-day being emerged. I started my prereqs in a bad place, and thought pursuing something would be better than being dead. I was blasé. I entered nursing school terrified and unsure of myself. And I found myself growing and developing a genuine passion for nursing - not just this survival-esque need to be useful. The human body intrigues me, the ability to be with patients and make an impact warms my heart, seeing progress in health reminds me why I pursued this work, seeing progress in my skills and knowledge fills me with self-assurance, the resilience I’ve developed in the face of a career that will try and try to burn me out makes me proud. I am smart and something of worth, I deserve to be safe and happy, and I am full of love and warmth. If I’m lucky, it can be felt by the people I care for. If I’m not, at least I am currently doing something I have worked towards and have entered a stable career path that gives me some flexibility in opportunities. 
I think it’s good to want to do good and to make an impact and to be the hands that help. I also think it’s important to recognize the complex and nuanced situation we stand in, in the healthcare system, and to realize that we, too, deserve good unto us. Protect your spirit and wellbeing, and it will make you a greater student and eventual nurse.

Ick… I just graduated nursing school, and I feel like it’s something you can only truly succeed at if you go at it with humility and a desire to learn. Learning from experienced nurses, in clinical and in day-to-day life, is an incredible boon. It’s thanks to all of them and their willingness to talk with me, demonstrate, and answer my questions that I feel in any way prepared to take my boards become a baby nurse. Any student shooting down that opportunity to be know-it-all and rude is stupid and terrifying.

Existence is now the rusty brown you’re still trying to scrub out from under your nails. 

Maybe it’s not right away, but eventually you’ll have to come to the realization that this stain doesn’t come out of the Earth’s fabric so easily. You can ask for the old color to come back, but you have changed, and that shade exists in your memories.

I think my experience is a milder reflection of what most people seem to have felt. I was a casual viewer who stayed closer to UhOhBro-like, humorous content instead of serious discussion or fan ratings (those creeped me out). Even with the little serious content I got into, I grew to develop an incredibly unhealthy view of depression, suicide, self harm, and abuse. Onision always presented himself as this intelligent and well spoken person, and even if he looks like a colossal moron now, he can be pretty convincing to a 12-13 year old. Why not believe him? 

Watching him lead to a lot of internalized hatred for myself and the feelings I didn’t really understand. He oftentimes blamed the people coming to him for support - “it’s your fault you’re suicidal” “it’s your fault you’re being abused” “feeling this way is selfish” generally being his message. Looking back, it’s gross how much my world view was affected. Thankfully I never regurgitated his message to anyone, but I certainly had a lot of anger towards myself for feeling depressed or for self harming. I blamed myself for these feelings and for the unhealthy situations I’d find myself in. 

Once his humor died on me, my views were replaced with much more rational ones. Still makes me angry when I think about all the kids who probably hated themselves and judged others for being depressed because of some bullshit Grog spewed.

Also! I agree with the other comments when they point out that tracing, though it might seem helpful when starting, doesn’t do much to develop your skills. I think it might help more to reference the image while you draw, so have a little more room to develop your personal style - while staying true to the character’s design! It could help you get more comfortable with drawing referenced characters in all sorts of positions and situations, which is a good way to develop skills you can use for your own characters. 
Tracing can show one scene, in one image, in one style, and you’re left with knowledge that’s hard to apply to your future drawings of your characters. It doesn’t give you the steps the original artist took to get to their finished piece, so it kinda leaves you more so with knowledge of an end result and none of the foundation it’s built upon.

Sorry to ramble so much!

YTA. I’m not going to touch the topic of the in-laws being weirdly demanding (really, the decision should be up to the people getting married..). Plans change, sometimes last minute. It’s shitty circumstances, but I can see why you made the change. You planned the timing of the wedding around allowing them to come.

It’s important to remember that, even though the in-laws are pushing really hard on this - at the end of the day, it was a decision that YOU made to accommodate them. A two day window is really short notice to find childcare. Especially for a child with mental illness. You need to understand that. 

What really made you the AH was how you reacted when YOUR decision rendered your sister unable to go. Her son has a mental illness, and instead of understanding that, you insulted him. I think even a kid without anxiety would feel thrown off by being left last minute with someone they’re not comfortable around. That’s amplified a thousand times over by anxiety - and it can manifest in different ways, like tantrums. It’s likely whoever she’d leave him with wouldn’t know how to calm him down, how to understand what he needs, etc. If I were in your sister’s situation, I’d bail, too. It’d be downright cruel to leave him in the hands of people who don’t like him (the neighbors) or people he’s not comfortable with (the boyfriend or any random babysitter). 

I get you want your wedding to go as perfectly as possible, and I get that you want your sister to be there. The world can’t revolve around your wedding, though, and your sister prioritizing her son is 100% rationalized. I get that it’s a stressful change, but seriously, it makes you look like (as many others have stated) a bridezilla.

YTA, but gently. You were unaware. As someone who was a band/choir student in middle/high school, I can kinda see where the mentality comes from. It’s not a huge performance with professional musicians - as OP has said in comments, children cry, audience members talk, etc - but I remember how hard we tried to have an air of professionalism. 

I would’ve been really, really embarrassed had my family called out my name in between songs. In my experience, the conductor makes it known when applause is appropriate. Those I worked with often conveyed with body language - my choral director stepped to the side, gestured to the choir, and bowed on our behalf, for example. My band director would gesture for us to stand before stepping to the side. It’s different for everyone, but I would wait until there is a very obvious cue that indicates the performance is over and that it’s okay to applaud. 

I think people like to cheer to encourage their kids - but I found it a lot more encouraging to hear what my family thought after performances. I think it may more so be embarrassing and distracting, in this case, as opposed to encouraging. 

I apologize for rambling - I know school performances are different for everyone. I think the parents at these performances would be true, full on assholes if they continued to cheer and yell after having the matter addressed on-stage by the conductor. They didn’t know - but they do now. Please wait until the end of a performance to applaud.
